questions.q: What is the central idea of the article?
options: Venus definitely harbors microbial life in its thick sulfuric clouds
Sulfuric acid destroys every organic molecule, so acid-based life is impossible
Life might exist in sulfuric acid, not just water, per the Seagers' work
Carbon is unnecessary because silicon can build the molecules of life
questions.explain: The Seagers' studies suggest organic molecules are stable in sulfuric acid, which could serve as a solvent for a different biology.

questions.q: Why did the rhododendron leaf survive in the sulfuric acid?
options: It was kept at a low temperature
Its waxy coating protected it
The acid was diluted
It was submerged for only seconds
questions.explain: The leaf's waxy coating kept it from breaking down.

questions.q: What did Dr. Seager's team find could replace sugar in the backbone of a DNA alternative?
options: Phosphate chains
Fatty acids
Silicon strands
Chains of peptides
questions.explain: An alternative to DNA stayed intact using chains of amino acids called peptides instead of sugars.

questions.q: With which company is Dr. Seager planning Venus missions?
options: Rocket Lab
SpaceX
Blue Origin
Boeing
questions.explain: She is planning a series of Venus missions in partnership with Rocket Lab.

questions.q: Why would photosynthesis be a problem on an acid-based world?
options: There is no sunlight reaching the acid clouds of such planets
Sugar falls apart in sulfuric acid, so it could not work as on Earth
Plants could not grow in acid at any temperature below boiling
Oxygen cannot exist near sulfuric acid, so none could be released
questions.explain: The article says sugar falls apart in the acid, so photosynthesis can't occur or must work very differently.
